\section{Threat Model and Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:threat_model}

A \emph{panel} $\mathcal{P} = \{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ consists of $K$ judges (with $K$ odd) that evaluate a candidate text via majority vote: the text is accepted if at least $t = \lceil K/2 \rceil$ judges approve it. Under an attack $a$, each judge $J_j$ is compromised with marginal failure probability $\eta_j(a) = \Pr(X_j^a = 1)$, where $X_j^a \in \{0,1\}$ denotes the failure indicator. We write $\eta_{\max} = \max_j \eta_j$ for the vulnerability of the weakest judge. The \emph{panel attack success rate} is $\mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a) = \Pr\!\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K X_j^a \geq t\bigr)$.

To quantify diversity, we define the \emph{effective independence} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ directly from pairwise mutual information (MI) among judges:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:keff}
K_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} \Bigl[1 + \sum_{j \neq i} \exp\!\bigl(-2 \cdot \mathrm{MI}(i,j)\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{equation}
This formulation computes effective independence from pairwise MI estimates without matrix decomposition, and is more stable for small panels ($K{=}3$). It ranges from $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx K$ when judges are nearly independent ($\mathrm{MI} \to 0$) to $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 1$ when judges are highly correlated ($\mathrm{MI} \to \infty$). Motivated by information-theoretic redundancy reduction, one can informally expect joint vulnerability to scale as $\eta_{\mathrm{joint}} \sim K_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \eta_{\max}$: independent channels multiply failure probabilities, so fewer effective channels (lower $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) should reduce panel vulnerability. This motivating relationship assumes non-adaptive faults and independent channels; it serves as intuition rather than a formal bound.

\begin{definition}[Adaptive Adversary]
\label{def:adversary}
A \emph{full-knowledge (oracle) adaptive adversary} has complete knowledge of the panel composition $\mathcal{P}$, the per-judge vulnerability profiles $\{\eta_j(\cdot)\}_{j=1}^K$, and the inter-judge correlation structure. It selects the attack $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$ to maximize the panel ASR, yielding $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P}) = \sup_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$. This oracle model represents an \emph{upper bound} on adversarial capability; realistic adversaries with partial knowledge of panel composition would achieve lower ASR.
\end{definition}

This departs from BFT models~\cite{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}, which tolerate $f < n/3$ faulty nodes but do not model adversaries that strategically target system structure. An adaptive adversary concentrates on the weakest link~\cite{schneier2000secrets}, suggesting a \emph{reversal}: under random faults, higher $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ reduces joint failure probability, but under adaptive adversaries, diverse judges may present a wider attack surface.

\begin{proposition}[Weakest-Link Monotonicity; formal statement and proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proof}]
\label{thm:monotonicity}
Replacing any panel member with a pointwise more vulnerable judge can only increase $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P})$, for any adversary including adaptive ones. The stochastic dominance condition holds for 58\% of judge pairs (61/105); non-dominance concentrates among within-tier pairs (72.1\% non-dominant, 31/43) versus cross-tier pairs (21.0\%, 13/62), reflecting that capability-similar judges lack uniform ordering.
\end{proposition}

The proposition predicts $\beta_2 > 0$ in Equation~\ref{eq:regression}. The independence-based intuition suggests $\beta_1 \leq 0$ under non-adaptive faults; the reversal pattern predicts positive $\beta_1$ for judge-specific attacks and negative for shared-bias attacks. The relative importance of $\eta_{\max}$ versus $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ depends on $K$: at small $K$, one weak judge flips the majority; at larger $K$, the adversary must compromise multiple judges. We test these predictions across $K \in \{3,5,7\}$ (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\paragraph{Condorcet Jury Theorem.}

\citet{condorcet1785essai} proved that majority voting accuracy converges to 1 when per-voter accuracy exceeds 0.5; \citet{ladha1992condorcet} extended the theorem to correlated voters, showing that positive correlation weakens the convergence guarantee. 42	
43	Our study has several limitations. \textbf{Diversity--capability confound.} The structural coupling between diversity and capability in current LLM ecosystems ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$; VIF $\approx 2.0$--$2.9$) is a fundamental limitation: observational regression cannot reliably separate their contributions. Capability-matched subsampling reduces but does not eliminate this confound (Pool~A $r{=}0.50$; \S\ref{sec:analysis}). Causal identification requires training-based diversity control.

Cluster counts fall below the ${\geq}20$ threshold at all panel sizes ($K{=}3$: 13, $K{=}5$: ${\leq}11$, $K{=}7$: ${\leq}9$ position clusters) \citep{cameron2008bootstrap}; however, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ remains bootstrap-significant at $K{\geq}5$ (7/12, 8/12), indicating that low cluster counts alone do not explain the attenuation pattern at $K{=}3$.

Each attack type uses 1--2 template variants; template-specific effects could confound attack-type comparisons, and conclusions may not generalize beyond the tested wordings. \section{Near-Chance Model Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:near_chance}

Two locally-hosted models---Qwen2.5-14B-AWQ (MMLU accuracy 0.253) and Qwen2.5-72B-AWQ (0.333)---score near the 4-choice random baseline of 0.25. A natural concern is that the positive association between panel diversity ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) and attack success rate is mechanically driven by panels containing near-random judges, which simultaneously inflate both independence and vulnerability.

We exclude all panels containing either model (MMLU ${<}\,0.35$ threshold), reducing the pool from 15 to 13 models and panel counts from 455/3{,}003/6{,}435 to 286/1{,}287/1{,}716 at $K{=}3/5/7$. We re-run OLS with BH-corrected $p$-values, the wild cluster bootstrap (WCB; $B{=}9{,}999$, Rademacher weights, max-$p$ across $K$ position clusters, BH-adjusted at $\alpha{=}0.05$), and the fractional logit GLM (Binomial, logit link, clustered SE with max-$p$, BH-adjusted). Table~\ref{tab:near_chance} reports FDR-significant $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ counts out of 12 conditions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Near-chance model sensitivity: FDR-significant $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ conditions out of 12 (2 benchmarks $\times$ 6 attacks). $\bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: mean standardized $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ coefficient across conditions.}
\label{tab:near_chance}
\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
\toprule
$K$ & Panel set & $n$ & OLS & WCB & Frac & $\bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$ & $\bar{R}^2$ \\
\midrule
3 & Full (15 models) & 455 & 11/12 & 3/12 & 8/12 & 0.349 & 0.340 \\
3 & Filtered (13 models) & 286 & 12/12 & 4/12 & 9/12 & \textbf{0.480} & 0.333 \\
\midrule
5 & Full (15 models) & 3{,}003 & 12/12 & 7/12 & 10/12 & 0.437 & 0.285 \\
5 & Filtered (13 models) & 1{,}287 & 11/12 & 7/12 & 11/12 & \textbf{0.512} & 0.256 \\
\midrule
7 & Full (15 models) & 6{,}435 & 12/12 & 8/12 & 10/12 & 0.401 & 0.244 \\
7 & Filtered (13 models) & 1{,}716 & 11/12 & 2/12 & 11/12 & 0.385 & 0.203 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

At $K{=}3$ and $K{=}5$, WCB significance is preserved or improved after filtering (3$\to$4 and 7$\to$7), and the mean standardized $\beta_{K_{\mathrm{eff}}}$ \emph{increases} from 0.349 to 0.480 ($K{=}3$) and from 0.437 to 0.512 ($K{=}5$), indicating that the diversity--vulnerability association is stronger, not weaker, without near-chance models. Fractional logit significance likewise improves after filtering at every $K$ (8$\to$9, 10$\to$11, 10$\to$11), confirming that the effect is not an artifact of the GLM specification. At $K{=}7$, WCB significance drops from 8/12 to 2/12; however, the combinatorial filtering removes 73.3\% of panels (6{,}435$\to$1{,}716), substantially reducing statistical power for the conservative bootstrap test. The raw WCB $p$-values at $K{=}7$ cluster in the 0.02--0.15 range rather than reversing sign, and the standardized coefficient remains positive ($\bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}{=}0.385$). The $K{=}7$ attenuation is therefore attributable to power loss from the sample reduction rather than absence of a genuine effect.

In contrast, $\eta_{\max}$ WCB significance drops sharply after filtering (4$\to$1, 2$\to$0, 1$\to$0 at $K{=}3/5/7$), indicating that the near-chance models contribute disproportionately to the $\eta_{\max}$--ASR association: their high individual vulnerability inflates both $\eta_{\max}$ variation and the corresponding WCB significance. Overall, the $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$--ASR association is robust to excluding near-chance models at all panel sizes, while $\eta_{\max}$ is not.

45	\textbf{Inference sensitivity.} At $K{=}3$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s significance is sensitive to inference method (OLS 12/12, bootstrap 4/12, fractional logit 9/12), though coefficient direction is positive in all 12 conditions. 47	\textbf{Benchmark and attack scope.} Both benchmarks use multiple-choice formats with discrete answer spaces; open-ended generation tasks (e.g., story writing, code generation) may present fundamentally different attack surfaces where continuous scoring replaces categorical judgments, and diversity--vulnerability relationships may differ. The six local models use AWQ INT4 quantization, which may confound the capability tier classification; two local models (qwen2.5-14b and qwen2.5-72b) achieve near-chance accuracy after quantization. Excluding these non-functional judges strengthens the diversity--vulnerability association ($\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.349 \to 0.480$ at $K{=}3$, $0.437 \to 0.512$ at $K{=}5$), indicating that near-chance models attenuate rather than inflate the signal; at $K{=}7$, direction is preserved but power is insufficient due to 73\% panel attrition (Appendix~\ref{app:near_chance}). Each attack type uses 1--2 template variants; template-specific effects could confound attack-type comparisons, and conclusions may not generalize beyond the tested wordings. All API models are accessed through OpenRouter, introducing a dependency on routing and snapshot consistency.

\textbf{Inference sensitivity.} At $K{=}3$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s significance is sensitive to inference method (OLS 12/12, bootstrap 4/12, fractional logit 9/12), though coefficient direction is positive in all 12 conditions. Cluster counts fall below the ${\geq}20$ threshold at all panel sizes ($K{=}3$: 13, $K{=}5$: ${\leq}11$, $K{=}7$: ${\leq}9$ position clusters) \citep{cameron2008bootstrap}; however, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ remains bootstrap-significant at $K{\geq}5$ (7/12, 8/12), indicating that low cluster counts alone do not explain the attenuation pattern at $K{=}3$.

\textbf{Benchmark and attack scope.} Both benchmarks use multiple-choice formats with discrete answer spaces; open-ended generation tasks (e.g., story writing, code generation) may present fundamentally different attack surfaces where continuous scoring replaces categorical judgments, and diversity--vulnerability relationships may differ. The six local models use AWQ INT4 quantization, which may confound the capability tier classification; two local models (qwen2.5-14b and qwen2.5-72b) achieve near-chance accuracy after quantization. Excluding these non-functional judges strengthens the diversity--vulnerability association ($\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.349 \to 0.480$ at $K{=}3$, $0.437 \to 0.512$ at $K{=}5$), indicating that near-chance models attenuate rather than inflate the signal; at $K{=}7$, direction is preserved but power is insufficient due to 73\% panel attrition (Appendix~\ref{app:near_chance}). Each attack type uses 1--2 template variants; template-specific effects could confound attack-type comparisons, and conclusions may not generalize beyond the tested wordings. All API models are accessed through OpenRouter, introducing a dependency on routing and snapshot consistency.
